At the outset, in order to consider the question whether prosecution has brought home the guilt to the Accused No. 2, it is to be noted that Complainant and Accused No. 2 are not Judgment KABC0A0012472023 strangers but closely related since Accused No. 2 is none but the co-sister of Complainant.

22. PW-5 to 7 are the police witnesses who have deposed about various investigation procedures viz.

23. Therefore, on analysis of the oral and documentary evidence on record, let in by the prosecution,
it is evident that only two incriminatory material are brought on record against the accused No. 2.
The first incriminatory material is the categorical and unequivocal say of complainant / PW-1 Judgment KABC0A0012472023 that the signature on Ex. P-3 is not her signature but is a forgery.

However, this evidence of PW-1 is diluted and in fact is nullified due to her own admission that she has signed the Compromise Petition marked as Ex. D-2, because in Ex. D-2, she has herself recognized the ownership of Accused No. 2 over Site No. 382 & 383 under the sale deeds dated 3-2-2010, which in turn are executed on the basis of the allegedly forged GPA.

In other words, by recognizing the ownership of Accused No. 2 over the two sites under said sale deeds, Complainant has ratified the acts of the GPA holder in executing the sale deeds dated 3-2-2010 in favour of Accused No. 2.
24.

27. However, the law is settled that expert evidence should not be given precedence over substantive evidence.

sentences.text: By now, it is well settled that the court must be cautious while evaluating expert evidence, which is a weak type of evidence and not substantive in nature.
It is also settled that it may not be safe to solely rely upon such evidence, and the court may seek independent and reliable corroboration in the facts of a given case.
Generally, mere expert evidence as to a fact is not regarded as conclusive proof of it.

In this respect, reference may be made to a long line of precedents that includes Ram Chandra v. State of U.P. [Ram Chandra v. State of U.P., AIR 1957 SC 381 : 1957 Cri LJ 559] , Shashi Kumar Banerjee v. Subodh Kumar Judgment KABC0A0012472023 Banerjee [Shashi Kumar Banerjee v. 28. It is well known that witnesses may lie, but circumstances never lie.

In this case, the manner in which Pw 1 herself has recognized the ownership of Accused No. 2 over the Site No. 382 and 383 in the compromise petition filed before court at Ex.D 2 and thereby ratified the act of the GPA in executing said deeds in favour of Accused No. 2 totally falsifies the allegation that the GPA is a forgery, because if the GPA was a forgery, there was no question of the complainant accepting the ownership of Accused No. 2 over the property on the basis of sale deeds executed by the GPA holder.

Therefore, only on the basis of the expert opinion rendered by Pw 4, it is not possible to come to the conclusion that the GPA at Ex. P3 is a forgery.

29. Apart from this, it is to be noted that, to bring home the guilt to Accused No. 2, it is not just enough for the prosecution to prove that GPA is a forgery, but prosecution has to further prove that Accused No. 2 committed the forgery in collusion with Accused No. 1 or that Accused No. 2 utilized the forged document knowing the same to be forgery, in order to cheat the Pw 1.
In this regard, no evidence is adduced to show that Accused No. 2 has anything to do with the forgery even conceding for sake of argument that GPA is a forged document.

The FSL report is crystal clear that the authorship of the signature on Ex. P3 GPA could not be established and this opinion is rendered although the sample handwriting and signatures of Accused No. 2 was also sent to FSL.

The say of Pw 1 to 3 that Accused No. 2 was involved in the forgery is only a statement without any basis and knowledge and is Judgment KABC0A0012472023 based upon the fact that it is Accused No. 2 who has derived benefit from the GPA since sale deed is executed in her favour but the law is settled that Varalakshmi V vs G Krishna Split Up on 17 January, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/47931909/

Therefore, on overall re-appreciation of the oral and documentary evidence on record, I come to the conclusion that prosecution has hopelessly failed to prove its case that the GPA at Ex. P3 is forgery and that the said forgery was committed by Accused No. 1 and 2 in collusion and Accused No. 2 utilised the forged document to get sale deed in her favour knowing the same to be a false document.
Accordingly the trial court came to the correct conclusion in acquitting the Accused No. 2 and accordingly I hold that the impugned judgment does not call for interference.
30. Before parting, it is necessary to take note of the grounds raised in the appeal memorandum.
Firstly, it is contended that the Learned Magistrate has committed error in dropping witnesses without issuing proclamation.
On perusal of the Charge-Sheet, it is noted that all witnesses Judgment KABC0A0012472023 cited in the Charge-Sheet are examined except 2 witnessess i.e. Cw 3 and Cw 6 have not been examined.
Cw 3 is the brother-in-law of Pw 1.

Even if he had been examined, his evidence would have been similar to that of Pw 1 to 3 and therefore his evidence would have been nothing but duplication and hence his evidence would not have any material bearing on the guilt or otherwise of the accused No.
2.
CW6, who is another witness who has been dropped, is a police witness who could only speak about certain investigative procedure performed by him during investigation.
His evidence is superfluous because when the IO is examined to speak about all the investigation procedures, the examination of subordinate police staff is not necessary.
Therefore, no prejudice has been caused to the prosecution by dropping of the said witnesses by the learned magistrate.

31. The other ground raised in the appeal memorandum is that the learned magistrate ought to have ordered for further Judgment KABC0A0012472023 investigation by directing the FSL to give opinion by verifying the sample signature and handwriting of accused No. 2 which was sent to FSL and by examining the Sub-Registrar.

This contention cannot be accepted because in so far as further investigation by FSL is concerned, when the FSL expert has clearly opined that the authorship of the signatures on GPA could not be ascertained because they are imitation forgery, the question of again directing further investigation by FSL to identify and establish the authorship of the signatures on GPA does not arise because the expert has already opined that the authorship could not be established.
32.

In so far as the contention that the sub registrar should have been examined as additional witness is concerned, it is to be noted that, what has been registered before the sub registrar are the sale deeds and not the allegedly forged GPA.

In this case, it is first necessary for the prosecution to prove that the GPA is a forgery and the said forgery has been committed by accused No. 2 or accused No. 2 used the same Judgment KABC0A0012472023 although she was aware that it is a forgery.

When this primary fact to bring home the guilt to the accused is not proved, the evidence of the sub registrar who has only registered the sale deeds is totally irrelevant for the purpose of the case.
Accordingly for all the above reasons.
I hold that the Learned Magistrate was perfectly justified in recording the judgment of acquittal and accordingly, I answer point No. 1 in the negative.

Point No. 2 :-
Varalakshmi V vs G Krishna Split Up on 17 January, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/47931909/
9 33.
Under IA No. 2, under section 391 of CRPC for additional evidence, the prayer of the appellant is to permit the appellant to lead further evidence.

The grounds raised are the same grounds which have already been considered supra and rejected viz, all the charge sheet witnesses have not been examined and it was necessary to call for further report from the FSL to establish the authorship of signature on GPA and for opinion regarding the specimen signature and handwriting Judgment KABC0A0012472023 of accused No. 2 and that it is necessary to examine the Sub- Registrar.
All these contentions have also been raised in the appeal memorandum and have been considered supra and rejected.

For the same reasons noted supra, the application for additional evidence also fails and I answer point No. 2 in the negative and proceed to pass the following :-
:: ORDER ::
The Criminal Appeal is dismissed.
IA No. 2 filed by the Appellant under Section 391 of CRPC is rejected.
Office to send back the Trial Court Records forthwith.

opennyai_summary.issue:
5. The points that arises for my consideration are as follows;
Judgment KABC0A0012472023 1) Whether the impugned judgment passed by Learned 11th ACMM, Bangalore in CC 54087 of 2016 dated 17-12-2022 acquitting the respondent no. 1 herein/ accused no. 2 of the offences under section 464, 465, 468, 471, 420 read with section 34 of IPC calls for interference in this appeal?
2) Whether IA No. 2 filed by the appellant under section 391 of CRPC for additional evidence deserves to be allowed?
6.
opennyai_summary.facts:
Thereby alleging the offences of forgery and cheating, the private complaint was presented before the Learned magistrate and the Learned magistrate referred the same for investigation to respondent No. 2, Hennur Police under section 156 [3] of CRPC.
10.
After due investigation, charge sheet was filed for aforestated offences against accused No. 1 and 2.
During investigation itself, the accused No. 2 obtained anticipatory bail and appeared before the IO while Accused No. 1 was shown as absconding in the Charge-Sheet.
opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
Firstly, prosecution has to prove that the GPA at Ex. P-3 is a forgery and it is not signed by the Complainant but somebody else has forged the signature of the Complainant on the GPA.
Secondly, the prosecution has to prove that said forgery was committed by Accused No. 2 or by Accused No. 1 and 2 in collusion with each other or that Accused No. 2 used the said GPA to get the sale deed in her favour knowing the same to be a forged document.
Apart from this, the said Judgment KABC0A0012472023 Compromise Petition at Ex. D-2 is dated 27-2-2017 and the evidence of PW-1 is recorded on 23-09-2021 after nearly 4 years and in the interregnum of 4 years, PW-1 has not filed any application before the court which recorded the said Compromise that the Compromise is a result of fraud.
Therefore, it is clear that with her eyes open, PW-1 has ratified the acts of the GPA holder in executing the sale deeds in favour of Accused No. 2.
Such being the case, the evidence of PW-1 that the said GPA is a forgery and she has not executed the said GPA does not have much evidentiary value and therefore cannot be the basis for coming to the conclusion that the GPA is a forged document.
27. However, the law is settled that expert evidence should not be given precedence over substantive evidence.
In this regard, reference may be made to the law laid down by Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Chennadi Jalapathi Reddy v. Baddam Pratapa Reddy, (2019) 14 SCC 220 :
(2020) 1 SCC (Civ) 514 : 2019 SCC OnLine SC 1098 at page 225, as follows;
10.
By now, it is well settled that the court must be cautious while evaluating expert evidence, which is a weak type of evidence and not substantive in nature.
It is also settled that it may not be safe to solely rely upon such evidence, and the court may seek independent and reliable corroboration in the facts of a given case.
Generally, mere expert evidence as to a fact is not regarded as conclusive proof of it.
In this respect, reference may be made to a long line of precedents that includes Ram Chandra v. State of U.P. [Ram Chandra v. State of U.P., AIR 1957 SC 381 : 1957 Cri LJ 559] , Shashi Kumar Banerjee v. Subodh Kumar Judgment KABC0A0012472023 Banerjee [Shashi Kumar Banerjee v. Subodh Kumar Banerjee, AIR 1964 SC 529] , Magan Bihari Lal v. State of Punjab [Magan Bihari Lal v. State of Punjab, (1977) 2 SCC 210 : 1977 SCC (Cri) 313] and S. Gopal Reddy v.
State of A.P. [S. Gopal Reddy v. State of A.P., (1996) 4 SCC 596 :
1996 SCC (Cri) 792]
11.
In Alamgir v. State (NCT of Delhi) [Alamgir v. State (NCT of Delhi), (2003) 1 SCC 21 : 2003 SCC (Cri) 165] , without referring to Section 46 of the Evidence Act,
this Court reiterated the observations in Murari Lal [Murari Lal v. State of M.P., (1980) 1 SCC 704 :
1980 SCC (Cri) 330] and stressed that the court must exercise due care and Judgment KABC0A0012472023 caution while determining the creditworthiness of expert evidence.
Clearly, these observations in Murari Lal [Murari Lal v. State of M.P., (1980) 1 SCC 704 : 1980 SCC (Cri) 330] and Alamgir [Alamgir v.
State (NCT of Delhi), (2003) 1 SCC 21 : 2003 SCC (Cri) 165] do not go against the proposition stated in Shashi Kumar Banerjee [Shashi Kumar Banerjee v. Subodh Kumar Banerjee, AIR 1964 SC 529]
that the evidence of a handwriting expert should rarely be given precedence over substantive evidence.
In this case, the manner in which Pw 1 herself has recognized the ownership of Accused No. 2 over the Site No. 382 and 383 in the compromise petition filed before court at Ex.D 2 and thereby ratified the act of the GPA in executing said deeds in favour of Accused No. 2 totally falsifies the allegation that the GPA is a forgery, because if the GPA was a forgery, there was no question of the complainant accepting the ownership of Accused No. 2 over the property on the basis of sale deeds executed by the GPA holder.
Therefore, only on the basis of the expert opinion rendered by Pw 4, it is not possible to come to the conclusion that the GPA at Ex. P3 is a forgery.
29. Apart from this, it is to be noted that, to bring home the guilt to Accused No. 2, it is not just enough for the prosecution to prove that GPA is a forgery, but prosecution has to further prove that Accused No. 2 committed the forgery in collusion with Accused No. 1 or that Accused No. 2 utilized the forged document knowing the same to be forgery, in order to cheat the Pw 1.
In this regard, no evidence is adduced to show that Accused No. 2 has anything to do with the forgery even conceding for sake of argument that GPA is a forged document.
In this case, it is first necessary for the prosecution to prove that the GPA is a forgery and the said forgery has been committed by accused No. 2 or accused No. 2 used the same Judgment KABC0A0012472023 although she was aware that it is a forgery.
When this primary fact to bring home the guilt to the accused is not proved, the evidence of the sub registrar who has only registered the sale deeds is totally irrelevant for the purpose of the case.
